paragraphs.source_en: The chronology of the Saharan rock art is one of the main challenges for the scholars and the source of persistent controversy. The problem relates to the oldest chronological-stylistic groups, namely the Bubaline, the Round Heads and partly the Pastoral styles; whereas the recent post-Neolithic paintings and engravings are chronologically secure due to the depiction of animals introduced to the Sahara in the historical period (Table 2-1). In the Acacus a few samples have been directly dated but so far there is no direct dating available for the paintings in the Tassili3. paragraphs.source_en: The relative chronology of the Saharan paintings can be answered by examining the stylistic superimpositions of the art which indicates the respective succession of Round Heads, Pastoral, Camel and Horse paintings. Although the exact dating of the earliest Saharan rock art has not yet been established, the absolute chronology can be constrained by the archaeology, by the animals represented and by the correlation with a scientifically dated palaeoclimatic and palaeoenvironmental record. Two humid stages occurred in the whole of the Saharan region at around 10,000–8,000 and 7,000–5,000 BP and these are generally believed to represent the main periods of prehistoric human occupation and consequently relate to the major phases of rock art production (Barnett & Mattingly 2003; Mori 2000; Jelinek 2004).

paragraphs.source_en: However, some scholars do not accept the existence of the rock art before the Pastoral period as they believe that the images of domesticated cattle are present in all chronological-stylistic groups (Muzzolini 1995a, b). The possibility that pre-Pastoral rock art production existed is the main area of dispute, leading to the two different chronologies being applied, a high and a low one.
